subject: Humanities
objective_verbatim: Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
focus: The Second World War in Europe. Conflict in Asia had already begun before September 1939.

LAUNCH Weekly - Spring.C40: Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
LAUNCH Weekly - Spring.D40_to_F40_generic: History of twentieth-century conflict and the Holocaust. Age-appropriate source work handled sensitively. Formative source/data tasks. Later causes/consequences evaluation in March. Opt-out respected.

LAUNCH - Spring.E10: Explain the causes and consequences of a 20th-century conflict; study the Holocaust sensitively; evaluate the importance of remembrance.

assessment_generic: Formative source/data tasks. This Week 1 practice does not establish later evaluation or qualification completion.
sensitive_response_route: You may point to PAUSE or tell the adult privately. Use the agreed supervised quiet place. You do not need to explain in front of others. When ready, choose a short private recap or the neutral date-order task. The adult will help you rejoin.
sensitive_context: Jewish people had varied ordinary lives, families and communities. Nazi antisemitism, prejudice and hatred directed at Jews, led to persecution before the war began. The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators. War and the Holocaust are connected, but they are not the same event. Nazi policy and human choices matter. Later lessons examine this carefully.
historical_name_rule: Real public historical people, events, places and dates may be named. No living private identities, pupils, staff, school or its local identifiers, website addresses, reproduced testimony or archive text. Model explanations are illustrative teacher-written and attributed to no real person.

sources.heading: Treaty and resentment
sources.text: The Treaty of Versailles was a peace agreement signed between Germany and the Allied powers on 28 June 1919. It took territory from Germany, limited its armed forces and required reparations, payments for war damage. Many Germans resented the terms. Nazi leaders later used this anger to win support for overturning the settlement.
sources.reasoning: Resentment gave Nazi leaders an issue to exploit. The treaty alone did not make another war inevitable.

sources.heading: Nazi rule and expansion
sources.text: Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor of Germany on 30 January 1933. The Nazis then destroyed democracy and built a dictatorship. Nazi leaders sought more territory and racist domination in eastern Europe. They rebuilt Germany's armed forces and made choices that increased the danger of war.
sources.reasoning: Nazi aims and decisions drove aggression. Responsibility belongs to decision makers and participants, not every German person.

sources.heading: Concessions failed to stop expansion
sources.text: At Munich in September 1938, Britain and France accepted Germany's takeover of the Sudetenland, part of Czechoslovakia. They hoped concessions would avoid war. In March 1939, German forces occupied the Czech lands of Bohemia and Moravia. The concessions had not ended Nazi expansion.
sources.reasoning: Appeasement aimed to prevent war but failed to stop further aggression. This response did not remove Nazi leaders' responsibility.

sources.heading: Invasion and the immediate trigger
sources.text: Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France had promised to support Poland. They declared war on Germany on 3 September after Germany did not withdraw. The invasion triggered a wider war in Europe.
sources.reasoning: The invasion was the immediate trigger. Earlier causes help explain why this crisis developed.

sources.heading: An enabling agreement
sources.text: Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union made a non-aggression pact. A secret part divided areas of eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Hitler could attack Poland with less immediate risk of Soviet opposition. The agreement helped enable the invasion.
sources.reasoning: This is an additional enabling factor. It does not mean the two states shared every aim.

source_card_status: Teacher-written factual summary for learning. This is not an archive extract or testimony. No real person is quoted.

model.label: Illustrative teacher-written model explanation. Attributed to no real person.
model.text: Nazi expansion was a major cause of the Second World War in Europe. S2 shows that Nazi leaders sought territory and rebuilt armed forces after 1933. This increased the danger because they could use force against other countries. The Munich concessions did not stop expansion: S3 records occupation of the Czech lands in March 1939. The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 was the immediate trigger, followed by British and French declarations of war on 3 September (S4). Several causes mattered. These events did not make war unavoidable or justify aggression.

success_criteria: I can name at least two causes and use dated evidence.
I can explain how each cause increased the risk of war.
I can distinguish longer-term causes from the immediate trigger.

hinge.question: Which answer explains a cause? A: The treaty was signed in 1919. B: Nazi leaders exploited resentment of the treaty to gain support for expansion, increasing the risk of conflict. C: The treaty made war certain.
hinge.answer: B. A gives a fact without a causal link. C claims inevitability without evidence.
hinge.rule: Check each learner privately. If either gives A or C, model fact plus because plus effect using S2, then use the parallel check before independent work.
hinge.parallel: S3 says German forces occupied Czech lands in March 1939. Explain what this suggests about the attempt to stop expansion through concessions. Answer: further expansion shows those concessions had not stopped aggression.

pair_work: Analyst chooses a cause and explains its effect. Evidence Checker finds the date and source and asks how it increased the risk of war. Swap after the first link. Each learner keeps an individual final explanation. Neither learner speaks for both.

evidence.description: Keep your own causal explanation with at least two causes, dated evidence and source codes, a because link for each cause, and the immediate trigger. All routes explain the same conflict. Choose a brief paragraph, linked notes, a directed diagram or a private recorded explanation with exact scribing.

communication: Offer to the Communication portfolio. Voice, adult audience reply, one NS and own response precede R. E follows actual banking.

next_lesson_reference_only.objective_verbatim: Study the Holocaust sensitively (Holocaust Memorial Day).
next_lesson_reference_only.calendar_note: Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January. The scheme themed lesson is retained without equating it with that calendar week.

Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
Use this plan for the LAUNCH pair in a single 40-minute lesson. Read the sensitive-response notes before showing the deck. Keep the work factual, calm and optional in response mode. No live internet or additional material is needed.
Outcome
Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
Prepare and begin
Open Slides.pptx beside this plan. Give Shared_Resources/Source_Cards_White.pdf or Pink, Vocabulary_Mat and one chosen route from Task_Sheets. Each learner has an Evidence_Sheet. Shared resources are in the lesson folder, not a separate download. Public copies use the same shared folder.
Check the usual supervision arrangement and agree a discreet PAUSE signal and supervised quiet place. A pupil may pass or respond privately. No required reading aloud, personal disclosure or cold calling. Do not improvise role play or show extra images.
Running order
Minutes
Action
0–2
Arrival and private access check. Agree the pause route.
2–5
Order 1919, 1933 and 1939. Ask how a fact differs from an explanation.
5–7
Share the outcome and success criteria.
7–12

12–18

Cover answers and sensitive responses
Tuesday 5 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
Essential answers
S1: treaty resentment supplied an issue Nazi leaders exploited, but did not make war inevitable. S2: Nazi aims and decisions drove aggressive expansion. S3: concessions at Munich failed to stop later expansion. S4: invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 triggered the wider European war; Britain and France declared war on 3 September. S5 optionally explains how the German-Soviet Pact reduced the immediate risk of Soviet opposition.
Hinge: Which answer explains a cause? A: The treaty was signed in 1919. B: Nazi leaders exploited resentment of the treaty to gain support for expansion, increasing the risk of conflict. C: The treaty made war certain.
B. A gives a fact without a causal link. C claims inevitability without evidence.
Check each learner privately. If either gives A or C, model fact plus because plus effect using S2, then use the parallel check before independent work.
Parallel check: S3 says German forces occupied Czech lands in March 1939. Explain what this suggests about the attempt to stop expansion through concessions. Answer: further expansion shows those concessions had not stopped aggression.
If a pupil needs a pause
Stop the demand and offer the agreed supervised place without requiring a public explanation. Keep an adult aware of the pupil’s location. Offer the neutral task below or a private short recap when ready. A pause is not a behaviour penalty and does not establish a completed history outcome. If the usual supervision cannot be provided, keep the learner in a calm supervised part of the existing space and seek support through the normal route.
Neutral re-entry task: put these everyday times in order: 08:00 wake up; 12:00 lunch; 18:00 evening meal. Then order 1919, 1933, 1938 and 1939 without discussing conflict. These are optional practice prompts, not evidence that the history outcome has been met.
Acknowledge distress without probing. For a disclosure, listen and follow existing safeguarding arrangements. Correct antisemitic falsehoods clearly: Jewish people did not cause the war. Avoid collective blame. Hitler was appointed chancellor, not elected dictator. Explaining causes does not justify aggression.
Nazi persecution of Jewish people began before the war. Jewish people had diverse ordinary lives. The Holocaust and the war are connected but distinct. Keep later remembrance teaching separate from today’s causal explanation.
Evidence and completion
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Retain the learner’s own voice and an actual adult audience reply, one NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode before recording R. Record E only after actual evidence banking. Record the actual response mode and help. A partner’s answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.

Own work/reference __________  Adult reply and NS __________
Learner response __________  Actual banking __________

Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01

Sensitive responses and planned access
Tuesday 5 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
Handling sensitive responses
Give a brief content preview: this lesson examines decisions that led to war and introduces the meaning of antisemitism and the Holocaust. Use factual, calm language. Avoid graphic imagery, Nazi-symbol activities, simulations and victim or perpetrator role play. Do not ask pupils to imagine being a persecuted person, defend persecution or debate whether antisemitic claims are valid.
If distress appears, pause the task, acknowledge the response without probing and offer the agreed supervised route. Do not demand an explanation to the group or require catch-up discussion while dysregulated. If a pupil discloses a concern, listen, use the existing safeguarding route and record only what is required in the appropriate private system.
Challenge antisemitic falsehoods clearly and calmly. State that Jewish people did not cause the war. Distinguish Nazi leaders, participants and collaborators from all German people. Explaining a cause never excuses aggression or persecution.
Jewish people had varied ordinary lives, families and communities. Nazi antisemitism, prejudice and hatred directed at Jews, led to persecution before the war began. The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators. War and the Holocaust are connected, but they are not the same event. Nazi policy and human choices matter. Later lessons examine this carefully.
Pause and re entry
You may point to PAUSE or tell the adult privately. Use the agreed supervised quiet place. You do not need to explain in front of others. When ready, choose a short private recap or the neutral date-order task. The adult will help you rejoin.
Neutral re-entry task: put these everyday times in order: 08:00 wake up; 12:00 lunch; 18:00 evening meal. Then order 1919, 1933, 1938 and 1939 without discussing conflict. These are optional practice prompts, not evidence that the history outcome has been met.
Planned adaptations
Cognition and learning: show one source at a time, highlight date and decision, give a worked example then fade the final link. Communication and interaction: offer quiet rehearsal, a because frame, pointing or exact scribing. SEMH: predictable sequence, opt-out and private feedback, with no cold calling. Sensory and physical: uncluttered print, White or Pink choice, enlarged copies and usual aids. EAL: pre-teach key words, use a bilingual aid and allow planning in any language before an accessible final response.

Supported
Use S1, S2 and S4 with private reading, a frame and two cause links.
Independent
Use S1–S4. Explain two causes with dated facts, source codes and causal links; explain why one factor is insufficient.
Aspire
Add S5 if useful. Compare causes, explain interaction and make a supported judgement without claiming inevitability.
Staff support and checks
I do: direct attention to one dated fact and ask what it changed. We do: require a contribution from each learner, then swap roles. Independent: withdraw the model, retain the source and usual aid, and record any prompt actually used.
Prompt ladder: 1 Point to place/instruction. 2 Ask short question. 3 Rephrase instruction. 4 Provide scaffold/choice. 5 Model first step only, then return task.
Private questions: Foundation: Which source names the invasion? Middle: How did expansion raise the risk of war? Higher: Why does the treaty alone fail to explain its timing? Passing remains available.
Parallel hinge: S3 says German forces occupied Czech lands in March 1939. Explain what this suggests about the attempt to stop expansion through concessions. Answer: further expansion shows those concessions had not stopped aggression.
Feedback and evidence
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Retain the learner’s own voice and an actual adult audience reply, one NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode before recording R. Record E only after actual evidence banking. Record the actual response mode and help. A partner’s answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.

It took territory from Germany, limited its armed forces and required reparations, payments for war damage. Many Germans resented the terms. Nazi leaders later used this anger to win support for overturning the settlement.
Resentment gave Nazi leaders an issue to exploit. The treaty alone did not make another war inevitable.
Think: How did this factor change the risk of war?
Research basis: H1, H2.
S2 Nazi rule and expansion
30 January 1933 and after
Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor of Germany on 30 January 1933. The Nazis then destroyed democracy and built a dictatorship. Nazi leaders sought more territory and racist domination in eastern Europe. They rebuilt Germany's armed forces and made choices that increased the danger of war.
Nazi aims and decisions drove aggression. Responsibility belongs to decision makers and participants, not every German person.
Think: How did this factor change the risk of war?
Research basis: H3, H4.

Evidence cards on the causes of war

White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S3 Concessions failed to stop expansion
September 1938 to March 1939
At Munich in September 1938, Britain and France accepted Germany's takeover of the Sudetenland, part of Czechoslovakia. They hoped concessions would avoid war. In March 1939, German forces occupied the Czech lands of Bohemia and Moravia. The concessions had not ended Nazi expansion.
Appeasement aimed to prevent war but failed to stop further aggression. This response did not remove Nazi leaders' responsibility.
Think: How did this factor change the risk of war?
Research basis: H4, H5.
S4 Invasion and the immediate trigger
1 and 3 September 1939
Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France had promised to support Poland. They declared war on Germany on 3 September after Germany did not withdraw. The invasion triggered a wider war in Europe.
The invasion was the immediate trigger. Earlier causes help explain why this crisis developed.
Think: How did this factor change the risk of war?
Research basis: H6.

Evidence cards on the causes of war
Tuesday 5 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S5 An enabling agreement
23 August 1939
Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union made a non-aggression pact. A secret part divided areas of eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Hitler could attack Poland with less immediate risk of Soviet opposition. The agreement helped enable the invasion.
This is an additional enabling factor. It does not mean the two states shared every aim.
Think: How did this factor change the risk of war?
Research basis: H7.
Careful context for later learning
Jewish people had varied ordinary lives, families and communities. Nazi antisemitism, prejudice and hatred directed at Jews, led to persecution before the war began. The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators. War and the Holocaust are connected, but they are not the same event. Nazi policy and human choices matter. Later lessons examine this carefully.
History evidence can help explain harmful choices. It does not excuse them. You may ask for a private pause or choose the neutral date-order task.
resources.Shared_Resources/Staff_Answers.docx:
Staff answers for causes and evidence
Tuesday 5 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
Use these answers to judge the learner’s reasoning, not to require a single memorised paragraph. Keep actual pupil responses and help separate from the teacher-written model.
Source checks and causal links
S1, 28 June 1919: the Treaty of Versailles restricted armed forces, removed territory and imposed reparations. Nazi leaders exploited resentment. This is a background condition that helped political mobilisation; it cannot alone explain Nazi decisions or why war began in September 1939.
S2, 30 January 1933 and after: Hitler was appointed chancellor. The Nazis dismantled democracy, pursued territorial expansion and rebuilt military power. Their aims and decisions are a major driving cause. Do not generalise responsibility to every German person.
S3, September 1938 to March 1939: Britain and France hoped concessions at Munich would prevent conflict. German occupation of the Czech lands showed expansion continued. This supports a claim that appeasement failed to stop aggression. The policy response does not excuse or transfer responsibility for Nazi aggression.
S4: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war on 3 September after Germany did not withdraw. The invasion is the immediate trigger for the wider European war. The declarations help explain its widening, not an excuse for the invasion.
S5, optional: the German-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 reduced the immediate risk of Soviet opposition to an attack on Poland. It is an enabling factor. The two states did not share every aim. Do not call this pact the only cause.
Illustrative model
Illustrative teacher-written model explanation. Attributed to no real person.
Nazi expansion was a major cause of the Second World War in Europe. S2 shows that Nazi leaders sought territory and rebuilt armed forces after 1933. This increased the danger because they could use force against other countries. The Munich concessions did not stop expansion: S3 records occupation of the Czech lands in March 1939. The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 was the immediate trigger, followed by British and French declarations of war on 3 September (S4). Several causes mattered. These events did not make war unavoidable or justify aggression.

Checks feedback and historical boundaries
Tuesday 5 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 1 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W01
Hinge and parallel check
Which answer explains a cause? A: The treaty was signed in 1919. B: Nazi leaders exploited resentment of the treaty to gain support for expansion, increasing the risk of conflict. C: The treaty made war certain.
B. A gives a fact without a causal link. C claims inevitability without evidence.
Check each learner privately. If either gives A or C, model fact plus because plus effect using S2, then use the parallel check before independent work.
S3 says German forces occupied Czech lands in March 1939. Explain what this suggests about the attempt to stop expansion through concessions. Answer: further expansion shows those concessions had not stopped aggression.
Likely errors and corrections
A list of dates is chronology. Ask how the decision changed the risk of war. A defensible explanation needs a supported because link. If a learner says the treaty made war certain, return to later decisions and alternatives. If a learner says Hitler was elected dictator, clarify his appointment as chancellor and the later dismantling of democracy.
If blame falls on Jewish people or all Germans, stop and correct the claim. Jewish people did not cause the war. Identify specific governments, leaders, policies and actions. Separate explaining causes from approving them. War in Asia predated September 1939, so keep the European scope explicit.
Judging the common finish
Across all routes, accept two accurate causes with dated evidence/source codes, an explanation of how each raised risk and the invasion of Poland as immediate trigger. Supported work can use exact directed pointing or scribing. Independent work can connect factors. Aspire adds a reasoned importance judgement, interaction or evidence limitation. Do not reward length without reasoning or infer independent reading from an adult-read source.
Sensitive response and evidence
Use the agreed private pause and supervised re-entry route. No graphic detail or historical simulation is needed. Distinguish the Holocaust from the wider war and recognise Jewish lives beyond victimhood. No pupil needs to share a personal connection. Follow existing safeguarding arrangements for a disclosure without public probing.
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Retain the learner’s own voice and an actual adult audience reply, one NS and the learner’s response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode before recording R. Record E only after actual evidence banking. Record the actual response mode and help. A partner’s answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.
Research basis
Historical summaries draw on The National Archives, The Treaty of Versailles, and United States Holocaust Memorial Museum Holocaust Encyclopedia articles: Treaty of Versailles; Adolf Hitler is Appointed Chancellor; World War II in Europe; German Prewar Expansion; Munich Agreement; Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939; German-Soviet Pact. Teaching approach draws on United States Holocaust Memorial Museum Guidelines for Teaching about the Holocaust. Institution and title references identify the research without website addresses or copied archive text.

Stage I do. 5 minutes.
Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
Illustrative teacher-written model explanation. Attributed to no real person.
Full illustrative model: Nazi expansion was a major cause of the Second World War in Europe. S2 shows that Nazi leaders sought territory and rebuilt armed forces after 1933. This increased the danger because they could use force against other countries. The Munich concessions did not stop expansion: S3 records occupation of the Czech lands in March 1939. The invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 was the immediate trigger, followed by British and French declarations of war on 3 September (S4). Several causes mattered. These events did not make war unavoidable or justify aggression.
Show fact, reasoning and trigger separately, then remove one sentence frame. CfU: ask each learner privately to identify what the because sentence explains. If a learner only lists a date, model one link before returning the task. Sources: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, World War II in Europe; Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939.

Stage We do. 6 minutes.
Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
Use the complete Shared_Resources source cards. This chronology is a concise teaching summary, not a primary source. S1 background conditions; S2 purposeful decisions; S3 diplomatic response that failed to stop expansion; S4 immediate trigger and widening. Multiple connections are acceptable when explained. Hinge: Which answer explains a cause? A: The treaty was signed in 1919. B: Nazi leaders exploited resentment of the treaty to gain support for expansion, increasing the risk of conflict. C: The treaty made war certain.
Answer: B. A gives a fact without a causal link. C claims inevitability without evidence.
Decision rule: Check each learner privately. If either gives A or C, model fact plus because plus effect using S2, then use the parallel check before independent work.
Parallel check: S3 says German forces occupied Czech lands in March 1939. Explain what this suggests about the attempt to stop expansion through concessions. Answer: further expansion shows those concessions had not stopped aggression.
Optional S5: German-Soviet Pact, 23 August 1939, helped enable the invasion by reducing immediate risk of Soviet opposition. Sources: The National Archives, The Treaty of Versailles; United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Treaty of Versailles; Adolf Hitler is Appointed Chancellor; World War II in Europe; German Prewar Expansion; Munich Agreement; Invasion of Poland, Fall 1939; German-Soviet Pact.

Stage Word help. 0 minutes.
Explain the causes of a 20th-century conflict.
Use the supplied vocabulary mat for reparations, dictatorship, antisemitism and Holocaust. Explain these calmly at a suitable point without introducing graphic detail. Jewish people had varied ordinary lives, families and communities. Nazi antisemitism, prejudice and hatred directed at Jews, led to persecution before the war began. The Holocaust was the systematic persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators. War and the Holocaust are connected, but they are not the same event. Nazi policy and human choices matter. Later lessons examine this carefully.
